05 · Service & AI

League Insights AI

Nov 2025 — present

A year of match history, aggregated and handed to a model that tells you whether you're the reason you're losing.

PythonFlaskaiohttp PostgreSQLSQLAlchemyAWS Bedrock Next.js 16Recharts
Read the case study

The problem

Every player blames their team. Existing trackers show you a scoreboard, which settles nothing: it tells you what happened, but not whether you caused it. I wanted something that reads a full year of matches and answers the question properly.

What I built

An asynchronous Flask API that pulls a player's entire match history from the Riot API, stores it in PostgreSQL through SQLAlchemy with Alembic migrations, and derives metrics a scoreboard can't give you: early-game gold dominance at ten minutes, midgame volatility, a consistency score, roam score, and comeback-versus-throw classification. AWS Bedrock turns those aggregates into a written playstyle profile, rendered by a Next.js dashboard.

The hard part

Riot's API is rate-limited and a year of history runs to roughly a thousand matches, each needing its own timeline call. Serially, that was unusable. I moved the fetch layer to aiohttp so requests run concurrently inside the rate budget, and cached aggregates so a repeat lookup never refetches. Then integrity: partial fetches were writing half-populated rows, which quietly corrupts every aggregate downstream. Adding checks at the model layer is what made the numbers trustworthy.

What I'd change

The backend sits on a free tier and cold-starts, which is the worst thing about it. Next: a job queue so a first lookup returns immediately with a progress stream, moving aggregation off the request path entirely.

Live demo Source

Backend cold-starts on a free tier. For an instant load, use a pre-cached ID: EMP#2005, Ash#69420, GoreToBore#000 or shamt#FUMED. Any other Riot ID triggers a full year-long aggregation and takes a few minutes.

04 · Application

E-Library Platform

Oct 2025

A borrowing system with real-time availability, due-date logic and role-separated dashboards for students and administrators.

Next.js 15TypeScriptPostgreSQL Drizzle ORMNextAuthTailwind
Read the case study

The problem

Borrowing is deceptively stateful. Two students hitting "borrow" on the last copy at the same instant must not both succeed, and nobody should be able to borrow a title they already hold.

What I built

Availability that updates live, with duplicate-prevention on the borrow path. Students get a dashboard of current loans and history; administrators get catalogue management, user oversight and library-wide statistics. Access is split by role through NextAuth, and every database call is type-checked at compile time via Drizzle ORM rather than trusted at runtime.

The hard part

Search fired a query on every keystroke, which under real load is a self-inflicted denial of service. Debounced filtering meant a query only fires once you stop typing, and cut redundant search queries by roughly three quarters.

What I'd change

Duplicate prevention belongs in a transaction with a uniqueness constraint, not only in application logic. It's correct under normal use; I'd rather it be correct under contention by construction.

Issue Tracker

Oct 2025

Authenticated accounts, threaded comments, and search that stays fast as the table grows.

Next.js 15TypeScriptNeon Postgres Drizzle ORMNextAuthbcrypt
Read the case study

What I built

Registration and login with bcrypt-hashed passwords and JWT sessions, full CRUD on issues, threaded comments with attribution, and protected routes gated on session state. Built on the App Router, with React Server Components fetching data and Server Actions handling submission, so the first render carries real data instead of a skeleton.

The hard part

Deciding what belongs on the server. The intuitive split (everything client-side, fetch on mount) gives you a page that flashes empty. Moving queries into server components and mutations into server actions meant rethinking where state actually lives, and it's the pattern I'd reach for again.

What I'd change

Detail pages need edit and delete; assignment and priority levels are the next features. Right now this is a well-built foundation rather than a finished product.

03 · Data

E-Commerce DBMS

Sep — Nov 2025

A normalised Oracle schema with a PHP front end and a Unix layer that can tear the whole database down and rebuild it from nothing.

Oracle 19cSQLPHP OCI8BashUnix
Read the case study

The problem

A lot of student database projects are really one wide table with extra columns. The point here was a schema that holds up under real transactional workloads.

What I built

Eleven tables across user management, inventory, transactions and feedback, plus three views (staff report summary, top-rated products, sales summary), normalised to 3NF/BCNF with referential integrity enforced by foreign keys rather than by convention. On top, a PHP interface with full CRUD, live search and validation on both sides. Underneath, shell scripts that deploy the schema, seed data and run the analytics suite from a terminal menu, so the whole lifecycle is reproducible.

The hard part

The analytics are where the schema earns its keep: a multi-table join across orders, customers and products, an aggregation over sales by product, and a subquery-driven query to surface top customers. Keeping those readable and correct is what normalisation buys you. Every query is parameterised and input sanitised, since PHP and Oracle is an easy place to write an injection hole by accident.

02 · Firmware

EEBot Maze Navigator

Nov 2025

A robot solving a line-following maze, driven entirely by hand-written assembly.

AssemblySensor I/OFSMMotor control
Read the case study

The problem

Navigate a maze with nothing but a reflectance sensor bar and two motors. No operating system, no dynamic memory, and no debugger beyond what you can blink out on an LED.

What I built

A finite state machine in assembly that reads the sensor bar, classifies what it sees (on-line, off-line, junction, dead end) and drives the motors accordingly, holding the line between decision points and committing to a turn rule at each junction.

The hard part

Sensor readings are noisy and the robot has momentum, so a naive read-and-react loop oscillates across the line and can fire a junction turn twice. Everything interesting was in the timing: debouncing transitions, and giving each state a settling period before it will accept another.

Source

01 · Logic

8-Bit CPU From Scratch

Jan 2025

A processor built up from registers and gates in VHDL, synthesised onto an FPGA and verified cycle by cycle against simulation waveforms.

VHDLQuartus IIFPGA RTL7-segment I/O
Read the case study

The problem

Build a working 8-bit processor from primitives. No CPU core to instantiate and no soft processor to configure, just registers, a control path, an arithmetic unit, and output you can physically see.

What I built

Two 8-bit registers with independent resets hold the operands across clock cycles and feed an ALU selected by a one-hot 8-bit opcode, so each bit picks exactly one operation. The ALU returns two 4-bit results with their own negative flags. A state machine emits a 3-bit state into a 3-to-8 decoder with an enable line, and three seven-segment decoders drive the results and a status readout. Everything is pin-mapped to physical switches and displays on the board. I built three ALU variants: standard arithmetic and logic, an alternate opcode mapping, and a parity check that drives a literal y or n.

The hard part

VHDL looks sequential and isn't. Signal assignments inside a clocked process update at the end of that process, so code that reads correctly produces its value one cycle late. Every bug here was found by reading simulation waveforms in Quartus and tracing signals cycle by cycle, which is a different debugging discipline from stepping through software.
